frame: true ecliptic and equinox OF DATE, geocentric apparent — Horizons QUANTITIES='31' (ObsEcLon), CENTER='500@399', REF_SYSTEM=ICRF. Quoting Horizons' own header: "Observer-centered IAU76/80 ecliptic-of-date longitude and latitude of the target centers' apparent position, with light-time, gravitational deflection of light, and stellar aberrations." This is the frame swe_calc_ut returns by default.
frame_note: ACQUISITION.md §1 calls this the frame trap and it is the right name for it. Pulling QUANTITIES='18' instead, or setting REF_SYSTEM to the J2000 ecliptic, returns positions in a DIFFERENT frame — wrong by up to ~1.4 deg per century of precession. At the 1800 and 2100 epochs recorded here that is a two-to-three degree error: large, systematic, smoothly varying with epoch, and very easy to mistake for an engine bug because it looks like a trend rather than noise. Both runners assert the frame string before they assert any value.
time_scale: jd_ut is JULIAN DAY IN UT, not TT/TDB. Horizons was queried with TLIST_TYPE=JD and echoed the epochs under a 'Date__(UT)__HR:MN:SC.fff' column header, confirming it read the supplied JD on the UT scale. This matters more than it looks: TT and UT differ by ~64 s at 2000, which is ~0.0004 deg of Mars motion but ~0.0096 deg (35 arcsec) of MOON motion — over a hundred times this file's tolerance. Both engines are asked for the same jd_ut (swe_calc_ut and eclipticLonSpeed are both UT-argument), so the scale is consistent end to end; a future anchor that records a TT epoch in this field would break the Moon first and silently.
description: Geocentric apparent ecliptic longitudes for ten bodies at four epochs spanning 1800-2020, from JPL Horizons. This is the first anchor in the directory that checks a POSITION rather than a frame or a clock: ΔT pins the time base and ayanamsa.json pins the sidereal rotation, but until now nothing external constrained where either engine actually puts a planet. The golden vectors cannot: gen_parity_vectors.py writes the backend's own output, so the backend is an unfalsifiable oracle there, and the property harness compares the two engines to each other. Both stay green if both engines are wrong in the same direction — which, since both now sit on Swiss Ephemeris, is a live possibility rather than a theoretical one.
independence_note: Horizons integrates a DE44x-class ephemeris; Swiss Ephemeris ships a compression of DE431. Common JPL ancestry means this is NOT the fully independent lineage that, say, a Moshier-series check would give — the two share the underlying dynamical model, so a fault in DE itself would be invisible here. What it DOES catch is everything downstream of that model: Swiss's compression residuals, light-time and aberration convention, frame handling, and this repository's own call sites. That is the layer our bugs actually live in. Recorded plainly so nobody reads a green run as more than it is.

anchors.uncertainty_basis: 1e-7 deg (0.00036 arcsec) — ROUNDING ONLY. Horizons prints ObsEcLon to 7 decimal places, so the printed figure is within 5e-8 deg of the value the system computed. The OBSERVER table states no per-row formal uncertainty, so no physical ephemeris uncertainty is claimed here; the room for two correct ephemerides to disagree is carried entirely by engine_allowance, which is where it belongs.
anchors.engine_allowance_note: 5 arcsec, NOT the 1 arcsec ACQUISITION.md §1 specifies. That figure was derived from a premise this repository does not meet: it reads 'Swiss Ephemeris tracks DE431 to well under an arcsecond', which is true of Swiss reading its DATA FILES. The pinned test configuration has no data files for the Sun, Moon or planets — backend/tests/conftest.py forces SE_EPHE_PATH to the vendored packages/astra-core/src/vendor/swisseph, which contains only seas_18.se1 (asteroids, i.e. Chiron). Everything else therefore comes from Moshier's analytic series, whose accuracy is ~1 arcsec in the modern era and degrades to a few arcsec by 1800. Measured against these anchors it peaks at 3.13 arcsec (Pluto 1800), with Neptune 1800 at 2.05 and the Moon 2020 at 1.25; everything else is under 1. So 5 arcsec is the envelope of the engine ACTUALLY under test, not a number tuned until the failures fit. It remains 1/12 of the 1 arcmin at which a longitude error can flip a sign or house, so it cannot hide a chart-visible error. Shipping the full Swiss data files would justify tightening this back toward 1 arcsec — see moshier_finding.
anchors.source: JPL Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System, Solar System Dynamics Group, Jet Propulsion Laboratory

anchors.engine_allowance_note: 5 arcsec, NOT the 1 arcsec ACQUISITION.md §1 specifies. That figure was derived from a premise this repository does not meet: it reads 'Swiss Ephemeris tracks DE431 to well under an arcsecond', which is true of Swiss reading its DATA FILES. The pinned test configuration has no data files for the Sun, Moon or planets — backend/tests/conftest.py forces SE_EPHE_PATH to the vendored packages/astra-core/src/vendor/swisseph, which contains only seas_18.se1 (asteroids, i.e. Chiron). Everything else therefore comes from Moshier's analytic series, whose accuracy is ~1 arcsec in the modern era and degrades to a few arcsec by 1800. Measured against these anchors it peaks at 3.13 arcsec (Pluto 1800), with Neptune 1800 at 2.05 and the Moon 2020 at 1.25; everything else is under 1. So 5 arcsec is the envelope of the engine ACTUALLY under test, not a number tuned until the failures fit. It remains 1/12 of the 1 arcmin at which a longitude error can flip a sign or house, so it cannot hide a chart-visible error. Shipping the full Swiss data files would justify tightening this back toward 1 arcsec — see moshier_finding.

moshier_finding: THE FINDING THIS ANCHOR PRODUCED, and the reason engine_allowance is 5 arcsec rather than the 1 arcsec ACQUISITION.md asked for. This repository does not compute Sun, Moon or planetary positions from Swiss Ephemeris data files. It computes them from MOSHIER's analytic series. The only .se1 file in the pinned configuration is seas_18.se1, which carries asteroids (this is where Chiron comes from); with no sepl/semo files present, Swiss silently falls back to Moshier for everything else. Nothing announced this: /api/health reports "ephemeris": "swiss-files" whenever the directory EXISTS, because _USING_FILES (ephemeris.py:45-51) is a path check, not a capability check. So the health endpoint says swiss-files while the planets come from an analytic approximation. Measured here, that costs up to 3.13 arcsec (Pluto 1800), 2.05 (Neptune 1800) and 1.25 (Moon 2020). For the product this is HARMLESS — all of it is far inside the ~1 arcmin needed to move a body across a sign or house cusp, and no reading changes. It is recorded because it is invisible from inside: both engines share this configuration, so the golden vectors and the property harness agree perfectly while both sit a few arcsec off the sky. That is exactly the fault class parity/anchors exists to expose, and this is the first time anything in the repository has been able to see it. Two follow-ups, neither taken here: ship the full Swiss data files (accuracy, at the cost of image and APK size) and/or make _USING_FILES report what it actually has rather than that a folder exists.
delta_t_prediction_finding: WHY THERE IS NO 2100 EPOCH, though ACQUISITION.md §1 suggests one. It was acquired, tested, and withdrawn on evidence. At JD 2488069.5 the engine missed Horizons by 13.83 arcsec on the Moon, 1.45 on Mercury, 1.03 on Venus and 0.84 on the Sun. Dividing each miss by that body's angular speed converts them all into the SAME quantity: an implied time offset of 23.7 s, 21.4 s, 20.5 s and 19.9 s respectively. Four independent bodies agreeing on ~21 seconds is not a position error — it is Swiss and Horizons PREDICTING DIFFERENT VALUES OF DELTA-T for a year whose Earth rotation has not happened yet. ACQUISITION.md §2 already warns about this for the 2050 delta-T anchor ('a prediction, not an observation ... or the anchor becomes a tripwire for the publisher's forecast revisions rather than for our engines'); the same defect infects any UT-argument POSITION anchor at a future epoch, and it strikes the fastest body first, which is why the Moon failed by ten times everything else. The epoch was replaced with 2020-01-01 (JD 2458849.5), which sits in the observed delta-T era and still gives modern coverage. Do not re-add a future epoch to this file without solving the time scale: it would measure forecast disagreement, not ephemeris accuracy, and it would go red on a Swiss release that merely updated its delta-T table.
coverage_note: Ten bodies (Sun, Moon, Mercury..Pluto) x four epochs = 40 anchors. TWO corrections to ACQUISITION.md §1's suggested epochs, both forced by evidence rather than preference. (1) The 1800 epoch is JD 2378499.0 (1800-01-03), not JD 2378497.0 (1800-01-01): Horizons refuses that date for two of the ten bodies — "No ephemeris for target 'Neptune' prior to A.D. 1800-JAN-01 23:59:41.3785 UT", and the same for Pluto a day later. Moving the epoch two days keeps the full body set at every epoch rather than leaving a ragged edge. (2) There is no 2100 epoch; it is replaced by 2020-01-01 (JD 2458849.5) — see delta_t_prediction_finding. Anyone re-deriving these must use the recorded jd_ut, not the suggestion.
